full_judgment:
AKM Sadeque, J.: These two Rules involve a common question of law touching upon the fate of similar other Rules pending in this Court. These Rules call in a question of law whether inherent jurisdiction of this Court can be invoked under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure in respect of cases from which appeals are barred by law of limitation. These two Rules are particularly concerned with cases under the Special Powers Act. The period of appeal from a judgment and order under the Special Powers Act, 1974 is 30 days in accordance with section 30 of the Special Powers Act, 1974. Both these Rules were issued to consider whether the cases concerned, appeal from which was barred by limitation, could be examined under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure and whether the judgment of the tribunal could be quashed. 

 6. The other case referred to is the case of Bangladesh Vs. Shahjahan Siraj @ Sirajul Islam, reported in 32 DLR (AD) 1. This decision, to our -mind, is not of much consequence because the principle laid down in the decision is accepted on all hands. By the majority view in this decision it has been held that, jurisdiction conferred upon the High Court by section 561A CrPC can be exercised by it for limited purpose at least in respect of pending cases pending before the Special Tribunal. It may be observed that at the time the appellate and revisional jurisdiction of the High Court over the Special Tribunal had been taken away but since then the High Court has been given both appellate and revisional jurisdiction over the special tribunal. Therefore, there is no reason to differ from the view that the High Court can exercise its jurisdiction under section 561A over the Special Tribunal which is now subordinate to it. But the question before us now is whether the case having been disposed of and their appeal being barred by limitation they are amenable to the jurisdiction of the High Court under section 561A of the CrPC. The precise question would be whether the instant cases can be considered as one coming under the third category of cases referred to in the decision in the case of Abdul Quader Chowdhury Vs State. On looking at this passage it become very clear that the High Court will not embark upon assessment of evidence considered by the Court below. Their Lordships have clearly observed that in exercising the jurisdiction under section 561A the High Court would not embark upon an enquiry as to the evidence which is the function of the trial Magistrate and it would not be open to any party to invoke the High Court's inherent jurisdiction and contend that on a reasonable appreciation of the evidence the accusation made against the accused would not be sustained. It would be for an appellate Court to assess the evidence; but in the instant cases the appeals have been barred by limitation, and an application under section 561A of the Criminal Procedure Code cannot be a substitute for an appeal. 

 8. Now it is not disputed that the appeal from the judgment and order dated 19.8.91 passed in the Special Tribunal Case No. 29 of 1990 upon which the present Criminal Revision No. 1155 of 1992 arises was barred by limitation. Mr. SR Paul, the learned Amicus Curiae. had invited our attention to sections 3 and 29 of the Limitation Act, 1908 which is to the following effect: 

 "3. Dismissal of suits, etc. instituted, etc, after period of limitation-Subject to the provisions contained in sections 4 to 25 (inclusive), every suit instituted, appeal preferred, and application made, after the period of limitation prescribed therefor by the first schedule shall be dismissed, although limitation has not been set up as a defence." 

 Section 29 of the Limitation Act is to the effect that: 

 "29(2) Where any special law prescribes for any suit, appeal or application a period of limitation different from the period prescribed therefor by the first schedule, the provisions of section 3 shall apply, as if such period were prescribed therefor in that schedule, and for the purpose of determining any period of limitation prescribed for any suit, appeal or application by any special or local law-(a) the provisions contained in section 4, sections 9 to 18, and section 22 shall apply only in so far as, and to the extent to which, they are not expressly excluded by such special law and 

 9. Mr. SR Paul has submitted that in view of sections 3 and 29 of the Limitation Act if there is any special provision given in a Special Act for preferring an appeal, section 5 of the Limitation Act shall not apply. He has further drawn our attention to section 30 of the Special Powers Act which gives 30 days limitation for preferring an appeal against the judgment and order passed by the Special Tribunal. He has submitted that since the schedule of the Limitation Act prescribed 60 days' limitation in scheduled cases, and under the Special Powers Act the limitation for appeal is 30 days the intention of those who framed the law must have been that after lapse of 30 days, the decision in a Special Powers Act case must reach its finality. Mr. SR Paul argues that the scope of section 561 A of the CrPC is not to supersede or transcend the law of limitation. 

 11. Mr. Paul has draws our attention pointedly to the words "Nothing in this Code shall be deemed to limit". He has submitted that the provision of the Code of Criminal Procedure could not limit the inherent power of the High Court to make necessary orders for ends of justice. But in the cases under consideration it is not the provisions under the Code which seek to limit the inherent jurisdiction of the Court. It is the law of limitation which limits the jurisdiction. In other words, it is the law of limitation and not any provisions of the Code that has taken off the cases out of jurisdiction of the Code sealing their fate. Therefore, section 561 A of the Code of Criminal Procedure cannot be conceived to give the High Court the jurisdiction to retrieve the cases from moratorium after they have been barred by limitation. The section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure has not given any new jurisdiction to the High Court to override other laws. It is easy to see that this Court cannot have any inherent jurisdiction to strike down the law of limitation. 

 12. Now Mr. Maudud Ahmed had strenuously argued that in the instant cases there was mis-appreciation of evidence and the facts and circumstances of the cases do not warrant conviction. The accused were at least entitled to the benefit of doubt. Again, in the instant cases the accused were not aware of the cases when the trials were held in absentia. They were never given any chance to defend and as such this Court in exercise of its inherent jurisdiction should interfere with the judgments and orders concerned. He argues that the period of limitation for appeal is very short i.e. 30 days and section 5 of the Limitation Act is not applicable. So the cases deserve interference. But for the reasons stated above, however deserving the cases may be, we are not able to invoke jurisdiction under section 561A of the Code to interfere with the impugned judgments in view of the clear legal position. We cannot act as arbiters meeting out justice irrespective of law. In this connection we are tempted to quote from paragraph 11 from Benjamin Cardozo's The Nature of Judicial Process, Yale University Press (1921), "The Judge, even when he is free, is still not wholly free. He is not to innovate at pleasure. He is not a knighterrant roaming at will in pursuit of his own ideal of beauty or of goodness. He is to draw his inspiration from consecrated principles. He is not to yield to spasmodic sentiment, to vague and unregulated benevolence. He is to exercise discretion informed by tradition, methodized by analogy, disciplined by system and subordinated to the primordial necessity of order in the social life." In the case of Bangladesh Vs. Abdul Wahab and others reported in 12 BLD 368 in course of discussion about the interpretation of section 5 of the Limitation Act their Lordships observed, "The fact that the petitioner might have a cause to be pressed in the appeal, cannot outweigh the spirit and philosophy of the provisions of the Limitation Act." This observation applies to our case also. The law of limitation is so inexorable that a person loses his good title on account of law of limitation. It may be desirable that something is done for the redress of the accused who lost their right of appeal and has very good case in their defence, but it is for the legislature to do. 

 13. Mr Paul, on the other hand, has submitted that when appeals have been barred by limitation the accused who have been convicted under the Special Powers Act may not be, when their appeal is time barred, without any relief in appropriate cases, viz when the trial is without jurisdiction or when the conclusion is absurd in view of evidence. They might seek relief under Article 102(2)(ii) of the Constitution in such cases. If it transpired that the court concerned had no jurisdiction to proceed with the case or the jurisdiction of the court has been exercised in an absurd or preposterous way, the accused might have recourse to the constitutional jurisdiction of the High Court. Again, he has submitted that in appropriate cases, the convicts might also have recourse to the provision of Article 109 of the Constitution which is akin to Article 227 of the Indian Constitution. He has referred to the decision in the case of war yam Singh and another Vs. Amarnath reported in AIR 1954 (SC) 215 to support his views. It was found in this decision that under Article 127 of the Indian Constitution the High Court can examine and interfere with the judgment of the Courts below. 

 14. Mr. Aminul Hoque, the learned Attorney- General who also appeared to assist the Court, has supported the submission of Mr SR Paul and further pointed out that section 491 of the Code of Criminal Procedure could be taken recourse to by the convict if he can show that he has been illegally or improperly condemned to jail custody. He has referred to section 491 sub-section (l)(b) and interpreted the words in' public and private custody' to mean that even a convict could be brought before this court for examining whether he has been detained without any lawful trial. The Attorney- General is firmly of the view that section 561A of the CrPC cannot be invoked for setting aside the judgments of the Tribunal Court appeal from which have been barred by limitation. Mr AFA Shahid, the learned DAG with Mr. Syed Matiul Islam, the learned AAG also supported the argument made by Mr. SR Paul and the learned Attorney-General upon our anxious consideration of this point of law, we find that generally section 561A of the CrPC cannot be taken recourse to in any case where appeal has been barred by limitation, if the trial has not been held without jurisdiction or in the face of legal bar. So far as the alternative forums suggested above are concerned, we find it appropriate to reserve our views. 

 15. Now, coming to the case concerned in the Criminal Revision No. 1155/92, the facts are, that while executing warrant of arrest in PS Case No. 12 dated 20.7.89 under sections 307/302 of the Penal Code they learnt that some unauthorised weapons were kept with the petitioner Mir Mohammad Ali and on search a licensed pistol and some unlicensed arms were recovered from the house of the accused petitioner when he and his wife were away. So far as the merit of this case is concerned the submission is, that the seizure list witnesses have not proved the seizure and the fact that the petitioner belonged to armed forces and had licensed pistol in his possession. So there was no illegality in retaining licensed pistol. The seized unlicensed weapons might have been planted by the enemies of the petitioner and there is reasonable doubt as to the complicity of the petitioner in the case. As a matter of fact, the law, as we have already discussed, has pointed out that the case cannot come within the ambit under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure. It is to be noticed that even if the question of limitation should not arise we could not assess the evidence and give the petitioner benefit of doubt in exercise of power under section 561A. In the case of Muhammad Samiullah Khan and another Vs. State, PLD 1963 (SC) 237 = 15 DLR (SC) 150 their Lordships of the Supreme Court observed:
